extracted.intended_audience: mechanical engineers / experimental scientists studying friction and abrasion (tribology); engineers designing machinery/ships in the early-industrial context
extracted.subtask_description: A laboratory and table-based experimental study of friction and abrasion (attrition) across a variety of materials (cloth, leather, wood, stone, metals), reporting apparatus, measurements, proportions of resisting force to pressure, and effects of variables such as surface, pressure, velocity, time, lubrication, and orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of velocity on friction
rubrics_metrics.description: Velocities were found to have very little influence in augmenting friction (Coulomb, Vince), except that cloth and woollen produce an increase of retardation with an increase of velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report whether friction changes with speed for each material; note exceptions (fibrous materials like cloth/wool show increasing friction with velocity). Include any irregularities in velocity (many trials showed 'velocities very irregular'). Mark trials that approximate uniform velocity (the text denotes these with *).

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of surface material and hardness
rubrics_metrics.description: The friction of metals varies with their hardness; hard metals have less friction than soft ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare material pairings and hardness when reporting friction. Use the reported comparative ordering (Appendix: brass on wrought iron ~7.312; steel on steel ~6.860; tin on tin ~3.305, etc.) and indicate how hardness correlates with lower friction and greater resistance to abrasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of surface area / extent of surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of surface very much increases the resistance for some materials (cloth experiments show 'three times the surface nearly three times the resistance'); other investigators (Rondelet) concluded extent of surface did not alter its value for stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure and report friction for multiple surface areas. Record cases where surface area scales roughly proportionally vs cases where it does not, and note material dependence (cloth vs stone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of normal pressure / weight per unit area
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction often reported as a proportion of the pressure (force required to move as fraction of normal weight). For hard metals without unguents and within certain limits (up to ~32 lb 8 oz per sq. in), friction may be estimated at about one-sixth of the pressure; but friction can change with increasing loads and may increase markedly when approaching abrasion limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report weight on the surface, weight required to move, proportion, and convert to weight per square inch. Examine linearity/nonlinearity across a wide range (14 lbs to 192 lbs and beyond were tested).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time / duration effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction is greatly increased by time (noted strongly for cloth). Time of resting (e.g., remaining 12 hrs) increases adhesion/starting resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include trials at different elapsed times and report changes in required starting force and steady motion. Note 'after remaining 12 hrs it took to move it' style observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface roughness / asperity / cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rougher surfaces require greater power to move (Rondelet); cohesion greatly influences friction; some investigators found asperity did not alter the frictional value for stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize surface roughness/cohesion qualitatively or quantitatively and report its effect; reconcile differing findings across material classes (stones vs other solids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material pairing / contact combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction depends on the pair of contacting materials (e.g., brass on wrought iron, tin on cast iron, cast iron on cast iron) with measured average proportions and ranked behavior in tables and appendix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report pairwise friction measurements, give averages and ranges, and summarize comparative orderings (Appendix table provides averaged proportions for many pairings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle of elevation / angle of repose
rubrics_metrics.description: Angle of equilibrium (angle of repose) is reported (e.g., similar stones ~30°). Less weight increases the angle of repose; increase of surface produces a very great increase in the angle of repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure angles of repose and compare to horizontal surface results. Note limitations if available weights are inadequate to start motion at small angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abrasion onset and behavior under high load
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a power/weight threshold at which metals abrade each other; beyond abrasion limits friction behavior changes (examples: tin increases friction when load above 8 lb per sq. in; experiments with very high pressure caused abrasion of hardened steel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and report the load at which abrasion begins, and separately report friction before and after abrasion onset. Use progressive loading tests (tables showing progressive increase until abrasion) and record qualitative signs of abrasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus construction and calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparatus must be accurately made and adjusted (strong table, graduated arc for elevation, accurate scale and weights, pulley, roller/axle constructions, bored cast iron block, accurate pivots, cord quality), and sources of friction/rigidity of the measuring system should be ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document construction, calibration, dimensions, range of motion, friction/rigidity of pulleys/cords, and any improvements (e.g., substitution of roller allowing longer descent). Ensure axes have full play to prevent binding. Time by a seconds watch and mark space passed on axle/block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication and reporting of variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many results are irregular; the text reports 'mean of 3 trials', marks experiments that approximate uniform velocity, and highlights variability across trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run repeated trials (three or more) and report mean values, ranges, and irregularities. Flag trials with irregular velocities and comment on possible causes (e.g., prior compression of fibres).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of friction as proportion of pressure and per-area units
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction is presented as the proportion (force required to move : weight on surface) and converted to weight per square inch for comparability (lbs per sq. in.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include the proportion, and the normalized weight-per-area measure. Provide both absolute weights and per-inch metrics to allow comparison across surface areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of lubrication / unguents
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments compare axles with and without unguents; lubricants (soft soap, tallow, black-lead) significantly reduce friction (specific reductions shown in Table IX and notes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the type and quantity of lubricant, report friction with and without it, and quantify reduction (e.g., soft soap reduces friction for bilge-ways to an experimentally observed fraction of the pressure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface condition changes under pressure (compaction/condensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase of pressure may scarcely increase resistance in some cases because surfaces become condensed and less liable to abrasion; prior abrasion or compression of fibres affects results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and report surface condition changes (compaction, beginning of abrasion) during the experiment and consider their impact on measured friction. Note if surfaces had been previously abraded/compressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and complexity effects for large machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale experiments and complicated machinery may show anomalies and contradictions due to irregular movements and difficulty of producing simultaneous actions; results can be affected by unreported elements and contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When extrapolating to large or complex systems, document sources of irregularity and missing elements. Prefer controlled small-scale experiments to isolate factors before large-scale inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation of contact (laid flat vs edgewise; broad side vs narrow side)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friction may vary with orientation of contacting surfaces; for metals it was observed to be nearly the same whether the load be applied on the broad side or narrow side (despite area ratio ~6.22:1), though generally friction is less with the broad side than with the narrow side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test different orientations and report any differences; note peculiarities for soft metals (e.g., tin) that may behave differently under different orientations once abrasion occurs or under higher loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of fibrous (cloth) materials
rubrics_metrics.description: For fibrous substances like cloth: friction diminishes with increase of weight; friction is greater with fine cloths than coarse cloths; friction greatly increased by time; velocities and results often very irregular (possible compression of fibres).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fibrous materials separately: run tests across weight, surface area, time-resting, and note fibre compression history. Provide commentary on irregularity and starting adhesion phenomena (adhesion > weight for small weights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report ranges, averages, and notable extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental tables give ranges (e.g., cast iron on cast iron laid flat varies from 6.58 to 7.53) and averages across pressures; remarks summarize these ranges and average proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full tables with ranges and averages, and include summary statements of typical proportions and limits for each pairing/material class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation of materials for low abrasion and low friction applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Steel's hardening and resistance to abrasion render it preferable for reducing friction in delicate instruments (e.g., balances); experiments and historical Mint work support that hard metals wear less than soft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When prescribing materials for low-friction applications, prefer hardened steel or other hard metals; cite observed comparative wear and friction data from experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of consistent units and careful numeric reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments use pounds, ounces, hundredweight and explicitly compute weight per square inch; space passed, times (seconds), and proportions are tabulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent units and explicitly convert to per-area metrics. Report times, distances, and derived proportions clearly, and indicate how means were calculated (e.g., mean of 3 trials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative summary conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthesis statements summarizing findings: e.g., (1) friction of metals varies with hardness; (2) hard metals have less friction; (3) without unguents and within certain limits friction of hard metals ~1/6th of pressure; (4) within abrasion limits friction alike; (5) resistance increases considerably from low to high pressures with extremes varying by pairing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear bulleted synthesis of generalizable conclusions drawn from tables. Identify limits of applicability (pressure ranges, presence/absence of lubricants, presence of abrasion).
